reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-six home runs projected at 23 years old, and the Statcast profile behind it isn't asking for faith. Caminero's 93.1 mph average exit velocity and 51.0% hard-hit rate translate to an xSLG of .521, and the 12.5% walk rate shows he's earning pitches rather than just swinging through them. The discipline isn't elite, chase and whiff rates sit right around league average, so the profile hinges on whether he keeps making enough contact to let that raw power do its work at full volume. If he does, Tampa has a middle-of-the-order cornerstone for most of the decade; if the strike-zone management erodes under sustained pressure, the home run total comes down and so does everything built on top of it.

reports.name: James Wood

If the swing-and-miss stays where it is, you're looking at a .263 hitter who slugs .524 with 37 home runs, a classic power-over-contact profile that still plays at full-season scale because the discipline is genuine. reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting profile reads like three separate arguments for the same conclusion: a .413 xwOBA, a 16.7% barrel rate, and a 14.2% walk rate that together describe a hitter who earns his damage rather than stumbling into it. The projection's .952 OPS across 689 plate appearances is the natural landing spot for a contact-and-power profile this clean, and the 39 projected home runs carry weight because the underlying exit velocity and barrel numbers are built for that kind of output. On the mound, the pitching Statcast profile is quieter but still serious, a 2.71 xERA backed by a 30.4% whiff rate that keeps hitters from simply sitting fastball and doing damage. The whole read hinges on health, specifically whether his elbow holds through a full season as a two-way player after Tommy John surgery, because if he's DH-only for stretches, you lose the mound half of a profile that almost nobody else on earth can offer.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power gap is the whole tension here: a 94.0 mph average exit velocity sitting at the 98th percentile, 14.6% barrels, 51.9% hard-hit rate, and yet a 28.2% whiff rate that lands at the 30th percentile. The bat speed and raw damage are genuinely elite; the question isn't whether he can hit the ball hard but whether pitchers can keep living in the zone he struggles to cover. What saves the profile from being a boom-or-bust riddle is the 11.1% walk rate, which keeps the .370 xwOBA honest even when the strikeouts pile up at 26.7%. If he makes even modest gains against spin or off the barrel zone, the projection's .852 OPS with 28 home runs and 32 stolen bases starts to look conservative rather than optimistic.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill

Merrill's 46.2% hard-hit rate and 10.6% barrel rate say the raw power is translating; his .444 xSLG sits well above what his actual .410 SLG delivered last year, meaning there's legitimate thump that the projection's 23 projected home runs is built on. The problem is a 36.6% chase rate that slots near the bottom of the league, pairing with a 6.5% walk rate to produce an OBP that the projection puts at just .297 — all that hard contact gets taxed heavily when he keeps expanding. If pitchers continue to exploit the zone-management issues and he can't tighten the chase rate even modestly, you're looking at a second-division regular who bats .245 and steals 27 bases to stay useful; if the discipline edges forward and the xSLG starts showing up in the box score, there's a genuine everyday player with real pop and speed here.

reports.name: Andy Pages
reports.published_report: The expected-batting metrics are pulling in a different direction than the raw contact numbers suggest. Pages' xBA sits at .270 with an xSLG of .440, both quietly above-average, while his actual exit velocity at 89.1 mph and 7.7% barrel rate land right at the middle of the league — meaning the production is coming from a 42.9% hard-hit rate and smart contact shape, not pure brute force. His chase rate is where the profile gets interesting: 32.7% is below average, but his walk rate of 8.1% hasn't caught up to the discipline the eye-test implied, and that gap is the thing to watch. If the walk rate climbs toward what his chase behavior should generate, the projection's .329 OBP looks conservative against 677 plate appearances and 27 home runs; if it doesn't, he's a useful everyday outfielder in an elite lineup, one whose plus speed and elite outfield defense make him genuinely hard to bench even in the down scenarios.

reports.name: Michael Harris II
reports.published_report: The contact quality here is genuinely striking: a .294 xBA and 49.6% hard-hit rate that together explain why the projection carries a .287 AVG and .490 SLG. What the Statcast profile also shows, honestly, is a 44.7% chase rate that sits near the bottom of the league, and a 3.9% walk rate to match — Harris sells out for contact against stuff outside the zone, and the strikeout number (19.1% K%) stays manageable mostly because he makes enough hard contact to survive the approach. The whole profile hinges on whether pitchers can force him to keep chasing and start missing, because if that chase rate bleeds into a rising whiff rate, the bat-to-ball skill that makes everything else work starts to erode. At full health over 620 PA, he's a true everyday outfielder with 27 home runs and a .808 OPS, probably underrated precisely because the walk total keeps the on-base number modest.

reports.name: Ronald Acuña Jr.
reports.published_report: The .376 xwOBA tells you the bat is still there; the 27.0 ft/s sprint speed tells you almost everything else has changed. Pre-injury Acuña was a weapon in every phase, and the legs were the multiplier — now they're ordinary, which is why a 14.1% barrel rate and 13.4% walk rate are projecting to 19 home runs and 24 steals across a partial season rather than the conversation he was having two years ago. The whiff rate sits at 29.4%, elevated enough to keep the batting average suppressed even when the contact quality is legitimately elite, and a .257/.367/.451 projection assumes he's getting to 479 plate appearances, which is itself a health assumption. If the knee gives him a full workload and the legs recover further, the .495 xSLG suggests a ceiling closer to his old self; if the speed number is the new floor, you're looking at a very good corner outfielder who walks and barrels the ball, not the singular player he was.

reports.name: Nolan McLean
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is doing real work here: 28.5 K% puts McLean in the 86th percentile, and 207 punchouts across 178.3 projected innings is the kind of volume that holds a rotation slot together even when the peripherals are mixed. The chase rate, at 28.0%, is the uncomfortable number — hitters aren't biting out of the zone, which means the strikeouts are coming from whiffs and called strikes in the zone rather than manufactured expansion, and that's a narrower margin for error. His xERA sits at 3.63 and the projection slots him at a 3.50 ERA over 18 quality starts, a profile that holds if the command (8.8 BB%) tightens just enough to keep him from falling behind and losing the zone advantage he's already not getting for free. If the walk rate stays sticky and the chase rate doesn't improve, he slides toward a back-end arm who survives on strikeouts but works too deep into counts to sustain the innings load.

reports.name: Bo Bichette
reports.published_report: The profile that keeps shortstops employed on reputation alone, except this one actually has an argument. Bichette's xBA sits at .275 while his xSLG is .406, a bat-to-ball skill carrying a swing that doesn't walk and chases at a 40.6% clip sitting near the very bottom of the league. The tension is that the contact quality is real enough to sustain a useful hitter, but that 6.0% walk rate bleeds the on-base line dry, and the projection lands accordingly: .261/.307/.383 across a full 693 PA season, a second-division regular who piles up counting stats in a good lineup without punishing pitchers who attack the zone. He becomes a reliable everyday shortstop if the glove holds, that 79th-percentile OAA keeping him in the lineup conversation on days the bat is quiet, but if the defense slips, what's left is a free-swinger whose power ceiling is 16 home runs.

reports.name: Colt Keith
reports.published_report: The profile splits cleanly in two: Keith's xBA grades in the 82nd percentile while his walk rate sits at 5.7%, a bottom-of-the-leaderboard figure that drags the rest of the offensive picture down. He makes contact, avoids chases at a 25.2% rate that grades well above average, and keeps the strikeout rate at a manageable 19.2%, so the hit tool is credible. The power is modest, 88.6 mph average exit velocity with a 7.3% barrel rate, and 13 projected home runs about captures what that profile earns. Everything hinges on whether he learns to take a pitch, because without more walks the .321 OBP in the projection is probably the ceiling, not the floor, and that lands him as a second-division regular with a real chance to stay there.

reports.name: Owen Murphy
reports.published_report: The MLB-equivalent walk rate is the one number Murphy needs to fix before the rest of his profile matters: 4.1 BB/9 across AAA & AA, translating to the same 4.1 at the MLB level. The strikeout stuff travels well enough, 8.8 K/9 in translation, and 107 strikeouts across 94 innings at AAA & AA shows the swing-and-miss is genuine. But a translated K-BB% of 13.0 against a 13.5 MLB average means the walks are already eating what the strikeouts earn, and that erosion gets worse when the competition improves. If the command firms up, he's a back-end starter with a real strikeout foundation; if it doesn't, what's left is a depth arm.

reports.name: Jake McCarthy
reports.published_report: The legs are the whole profile. At 29.9 ft/s sprint speed, McCarthy sits at the 99th percentile, and that engine is what makes a .310 xwOBA and 85.0 mph average exit velocity, both in the bottom handful of the league, survivable as a projection. The Statcast contact shape is genuinely curious: his xBA grades out at the 76th percentile while hard-hit rate sits at just 4.7%, which says he's making contact but almost never driving the ball, turning weak grounders and liners into hits that most hitters can't leg out. The projection's .290/.332/.472 line with 25 stolen bases is essentially the optimistic version of that profile, one that requires Coors Field to inflate the raw output and the speed to keep converting soft contact into base hits at an unsustainable clip. If either of those conditions softens, you're looking at a useful fourth outfielder with plus speed rather than a near-everyday player.

reports.name: Leo De Vries
reports.published_report: The bat-to-ball reads loud at 19 in Double-A: .289 at AA with a 12% walk rate and 33 stolen bases in 414 plate appearances is a profile that earns attention. The contact holds up in translation, but the power softens considerably — his .166 ISO at AA becomes .134 in MLB equivalent, a tick below league average, and that gap is where the ceiling question lives. If the speed and on-base skills (.379 OBP at AA) carry to the majors and the power stays modest, he's a useful bench or platoon piece; if the hit tool slips when the pitching quality jumps, there's not enough thump to carry the profile. A bench bat with legs, one to two years out, and the ceiling hinges entirely on whether the contact rate survives the leap.

He's a pure bat-to-ball profile that doesn't punish barrels, and the 4.2% walk rate means he needs the singles to keep coming because there's no secondary on-base cushion to lean on. If the hit tool keeps translating, he's a .295 average everyday outfielder who won't hurt you; if the contact rate regresses even slightly, there isn't enough power or patience underneath to hold the lineup spot.

His 20% strikeout rate in the Pacific Coast environment translates to 21.4% against big-league pitching, a tick below the 22.0% mark MLB hitters post, and his walk rate comes through at 9.8% translated, above what the average MLB hitter draws. The bat plays; the question is how much it plays at catcher specifically, because the .203 ISO in AAA softens to .157 translated, which is right at the MLB average of .150 and nothing more. If he holds that contact quality behind the plate and the walk rate doesn't erode, he's a real backup with some starting days; if the discipline slips under major-league spin, the profile narrows to a bench piece who earns his roster spot with the glove.

reports.published_report: The ISO is the loudest thing in this profile, and it demands some skepticism. The 22 home runs and 22 stolen beans for a 19-year-old center fielder are genuinely loud, but the 29 K% at A+ becomes 31.2% in the MLB-equivalent read, well above the 22.0% pool norm, and that's the whole problem. If the contact rate doesn't tighten as competition improves, the ceiling closes: either a fringe everyday bat who survives on the power-speed combination, or the strikeouts eat him alive and he's a bench piece with loud tools and a limited role.

reports.name: Dustin May
reports.published_report: The fastball grades out beautifully, 96.9 mph and 2326 rpm, and then the contact suppression profile refuses to follow. A 45.7% hard-hit rate and 90.1 mph average exit velocity against him are genuinely ugly numbers, which is the central tension in everything Dustin May does: he can blow it by hitters at the point of offering, but the ones who make contact hit it hard. The strikeout and walk rates sit right at league average, the xERA lands at 4.04, and the projection calls for a 4.26 ERA over 161.3 innings, so what you're looking at is a mid-rotation profile built on a premium fastball that hasn't found a way to make the contact profile match. If he ever pairs that velocity and spin with a secondary that generates whiffs, his 22.6% whiff rate sits well below average and that gap is where the ceiling lives; if he doesn't, he's a reliable innings-eater and not much more.

reports.name: Cam Smith
reports.published_report: The barrel rate and speed are doing a lot of heavy lifting here. Smith's 11.6% barrel rate sits well above average contact quality, and his 29.2 ft/s sprint speed puts him in elite company on the bases, but a 28.4% whiff rate drags the whole profile back toward ordinary — that's the tension. The .331 xwOBA says the underlying contact is better than his actual results, and the .440 xSLG shows genuine pop, yet the strikeout rate is eating the walk rate alive, leaving an OBP projection of .298 that limits how much of the speed actually matters. Tighten the zone even modestly at 23 and the power-speed combination points toward an everyday outfielder; if the whiff rate holds, he's a second-division regular who gives you highlight reel moments between strikeouts.

reports.name: Caleb Durbin
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is almost entirely about what he doesn't do wrong. A 15.1% whiff rate and 13.2% strikeout rate put him in genuinely elite bat-to-ball territory, but an 84.1 mph average exit velocity at the 2nd percentile and a 2.9% barrel rate mean he makes contact with almost no damage attached to it. The .288 xwOBA tells you where that leaves him: a hitter who controls the zone well enough to stay in lineups but can't hurt you when he finds the barrel. The projection's 15 home runs across a full season hinge entirely on whether the counting-stat context, sprint speed, and base-running (19 projected steals) can paper over a power profile that the Statcast data suggests is closer to replacement than the slash line implies. The whole profile works as a useful bench contributor or a speed-and-defense piece in a creative lineup; it collapses into a sub-replacement bat the moment the contact efficiency dips even slightly, because there's no raw power to carry him through cold stretches.

reports.name: Rainiel Rodriguez
reports.published_report: Nineteen years old, catching in Double-A, and already posting an .899 OPS across AA & A+ through 401 plate appearances. The bat is the whole argument: .292/.386/.513 with 18 home runs and 46 walks, a profile that grades at the 91st percentile for OPS and 85th for ISO against the full hitter pool. Translate it to the majors and the power softens to a .159 ISO sitting just above league average, and the strikeout rate ticks up to 24.4% — which is the real hinge, because the ceiling here tops out as a platoon bat and the floor is bench depth, so if that K rate climbs further as the pitching sharpens, the power advantage that makes this profile interesting starts to thin out fast. For a 19-year-old catcher with 10 steals and a walk rate that translates cleanly, the production is loud enough; the question is whether the hit tool holds at the next level, not whether the skill is there now.

At 92.4 mph average exit velocity with a 52.8% hard-hit rate, Eldridge hits the ball as hard as almost anyone — the xSLG of .461 and a 12.8% walk rate show that the raw power and plate discipline are translating into real damage when he makes contact. The problem is a 26.6% strikeout rate that keeps the batting average suppressed, which is why the projection lands at .247/.336/.427 across 481 PA despite the loud contact numbers. If he can trim the strikeouts without sacrificing the walk rate or the exit velocity, he's a genuine middle-of-the-order first baseman; if the swing-and-miss stays where it is, you've got a low-end regular who needs the home run total to climb past 18 to justify the lineup spot.

reports.name: Travis Bazzana
reports.published_report: The profile splits almost perfectly down the middle, and that's the problem. Bazzana's 11.8% walk rate sits at the 80th percentile, his chase rate of 26.5% grades even better, and those two numbers together describe a hitter who genuinely understands the strike zone. Everything he does with a pitch he decides to swing at is a different story: a 4.3% barrel rate, an xBA of .224, an xSLG of .345, all sitting in the bottom fifth of the league, suggesting the contact quality isn't close to catching up to the plate discipline. The projection absorbs that tension and lands on a .337 OBP with modest pop, 13 home runs and 23 steals across 523 plate appearances, which is a useful player if the speed and on-base skills carry the line, and a roster problem if pitchers ever adjust to the swing decisions he's making on balls he chases. At 23, there's room for the bat-to-ball piece to develop, but right now the Statcast contact profile says he's a good walker who doesn't punish mistakes.

reports.name: Justin Wrobleski
reports.published_report: The 3.57 ERA projection and the 4.51 xERA are telling two different stories, and the Statcast profile sides firmly with the latter. His 5.1% walk rate is genuinely elite, 95th percentile, and his 32.4% chase rate does real work keeping counts in his favor, but a 19.6% whiff rate and a 43.3% hard-hit rate say batters who do make contact are hitting it hard and often. The 2447 rpm fastball spin is a legitimate carrying tool, and if that translates to more bat-miss at the top of the zone, the gap between the ERA and xERA narrows; if it doesn't, the soft-contact model that bridges them never materializes. Mid-rotation numbers on a surface read, back-end reality underneath: the walk rate keeps him in games, but the profile needs an out-pitch to hold there.

reports.name: Kahlil Watson
reports.published_report: The ceiling question here isn't power — it's contact. Watson is hitting .252 at AAA with 14 home runs and 18 stolen bases in 316 plate appearances, which is a real skill set for a 23-year-old center fielder, but his 28% strikeout rate translates to 27.2% against big-league pitching, well above a league average that sits around 22%. The walk rate translates to 11.1% at the MLB level, which is genuinely plus and keeps his OBP propped at .365 despite the contact noise. If the strikeout rate hardens into who he is rather than where he is developmentally, this profile resolves as a bench piece with pop and speed, not a regular; if he finds a way to cut the whiffs without sacrificing the .221 ISO, the speed and power combination gives him everyday upside.

reports.name: Garrett Mitchell

Jump's fastball sits at 96.2 mph with 2356 rpm of spin, and his 5.5% barrel rate shows hitters genuinely struggle to do damage when they do make contact — but a 10.8% walk rate undercuts all of it, keeping his xERA at 4.27 despite strikeout and contact-quality numbers that should belong to a better pitcher. The strikeouts are real enough, 25.3% K rate against a whiff percentage right at league average, which tells you the heater and spin are doing work even if the swing-and-miss isn't elite. If he tightens the zone, this profile has a mid-rotation floor; if he doesn't, the projection's 1.44 WHIP and 4.47 ERA are probably what you get, a guy who can miss enough bats to stay in a rotation but never quite turn the stuff into results.

reports.name: Josh Hartle
reports.published_report: The walk control is doing real work here. Hartle carries a 3.4 BB/9 at AA that translates to 3.6 at the MLB level, essentially average, but his strikeout rate tells the other side of the story: 8.7 K/9 at AA translates to 7.6, a full run below what MLB starters typically post. That gap is the whole profile. He misses enough bats to stay respectable, and at 23 with 98.7 innings of a 3.70 ERA at AA he has shown he can hold a rotation slot at this level, but if the command edge softens against better hitters, there isn't a swing-and-miss floor to catch him, and the ceiling tops out as a multi-inning reliever rather than anything deeper in a staff.

reports.name: Manny Machado
reports.published_report: Thirty-one home runs and 96 RBI at a .736 OPS is a profile that's useful but no longer dominant, and the Statcast card explains why. The exit velocity and hard-hit rate are solidly above average, the barrel rate at 10.6% holds up, and his 11.4% walk rate is genuinely good — but the xBA sits at .240, meaning the contact quality doesn't translate to average because the batted-ball shape isn't doing him favors. The projection's .223 AVG isn't bad luck waiting to correct; it's roughly what the underlying contact profile earns. What keeps him a legitimate middle-of-the-order piece at 34 is that the power and discipline are real enough to generate run production even when the batting average drags, and an 88th-percentile OAA mark means the defense at third is still an asset the lineup cost doesn't have to carry.

reports.name: Nasim Nuñez
reports.published_report: 52 projected steals on a .592 OPS is the whole profile in one breath. The contact and power metrics are nearly off the bottom of the chart, with 84.6 mph average exit velocity, a 0.4% barrel rate, and an xSLG of .270, and none of that gets better if pitchers decide to attack him, because his 25.7% chase rate and 10.7% walk rate already represent the ceiling of his plate discipline. What saves him as a roster piece is 29.8 ft/s sprint speed, which puts him in genuine elite company on the bases, paired with fielding that grades well at both middle-infield spots. He's a late-inning defensive replacement and pinch-runner who can start if a team is desperate for a shortstop, not a second-division regular, unless someone decides that stolen bases alone justify 518 plate appearances, which is a bet most front offices won't make.

reports.name: LuJames Groover
reports.published_report: The contact is undeniable at this level: a .308/.398/.464 line at AAA across 362 plate appearances, with 47 walks against 60 strikeouts, reads less like a hot streak and more like a disciplined hitter who simply makes the ball find the barrel. The translation softens it, as it always does — that strikeout rate becomes 19.4% where most MLB hitters sit at 22.0%, and the walk rate lands at 10.7% against a pool that averages 8.5%, so the plate discipline carries over clean. The power doesn't translate as cleanly: an ISO of .156 at AAA becomes .134 in equivalent terms, and six home runs in 362 plate appearances suggests Groover is a contact-and-walk profile first, with the pop needing a real jump to matter. If the bat-to-ball and the walk rate hold at the big-league level, he's a useful bench piece who can play in a platoon; if they don't, the below-average raw power leaves very little margin.

reports.name: Ian Seymour
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is built almost entirely on swing-and-miss, and the fastball is the part that doesn't fit. A 28.4% strikeout rate and 29.2% whiff rate are genuine, because the chase numbers back them up — hitters swing at 33.2% of pitches outside the zone, and that's what makes the strikeouts work without elite velocity. The fastball sits 91.5 mph and generates almost no spin, which means the barrel rate of 9.7% is the one number he can't sustain if the pitch selection or sequencing ever breaks down. The xERA of 3.48 is well below the 4.23 projection, and the gap is the whole argument: Seymour profiles as a back-end starter who misses bats at a rate that outpaces what his stuff looks like on paper, but he's one hard stretch of contact luck away from being a full-time reliever in Tampa's mix.

reports.name: Nathan Flewelling
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the problem. At A+ across 421 plate appearances, Flewelling has drawn 66 walks against 112 strikeouts, a 16% walk rate that grades 84th percentile in his pool, but the strikeouts translate to 29.6% at the MLB level while the ISO equivalent lands at .144, nearly identical to what a league-average hitter produces. A 19-year-old catcher who can take a walk is worth developing, but the ceiling here is narrow: if the strikeouts compress and the raw power that shows up as .207 ISO at A+ doesn't travel, what's left is a bench backstop with a good eye.

reports.name: Carlos Lagrange

The walk trouble is just as real — 33 free passes in that same stretch translates to a 4.2 BB/9, and that gap between his strikeout ceiling and his control floor is exactly why a near-elite punch rate produces a K-BB% that lands at barely 13.9% in MLB terms, right against the 13.5% mean. The whole profile hinges on whether he can tighten the zone enough to let the strikeout stuff breathe; if he can't, the depth-arm ceiling in his profile is the honest outcome, not a pessimistic one.

reports.name: Noah Cameron
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 4.39 and the fastball averages 92.5 mph, which puts him near the bottom fifth of starters by velocity. What keeps him functional is a walk rate of 7.6% that grades better than most of the rotation, and a 25.7% whiff rate that's roughly league-average, meaning hitters make contact but don't always punish it badly. The 29.1% chase rate is the soft spot: he can't expand the zone reliably, so the whiffs he gets come mostly from pitches over the plate, which is a narrow margin when the fastball already plays short. If the command holds and he sequences well enough to keep barrels down from that 8.7% figure, he's a back-end starter logging innings on a young Royals club; if the fastball gets elevated or the chase rate dips further, he slides into a bulk-inning role pretty quickly.

reports.name: Brandon Sproat
reports.published_report: The fastball sits 96.7 mph, which is a genuine weapon, and then almost everything else on the Statcast card falls apart. His 11.6% walk rate is the real damage: hitters barely need to chase him at 25.5% because he'll eventually find the zone on his terms, and when he does, they're hitting it hard — 43.1% hard-hit rate with an xERA of 4.84 that the 4.96 projection is basically copying faithfully. The strikeout rate at 24.2% is functional, not special, and his whiff rate of 25.1% suggests the fastball isn't missing enough bats to cover for the command problem. This works as a back-end innings-eater if the walk rate drops toward the league neighborhood; if it stays at 11.6%, he's a liability Milwaukee will cycle through the rotation out of necessity rather than conviction.

reports.name: Javier Sanoja
reports.published_report: The contact profile is legitimate and the power profile is not. Sanoja's 7.7% strikeout rate is essentially the floor of the leaderboard, and an 11.6% whiff rate that elite means he's genuinely hard to miss, but a 1.9% barrel rate and 86.7 mph average exit velocity explain why the projection lands at .269/.308/.404 despite all that contact: he's putting the ball in play without doing much with it. The whole thing hinges on whether he generates enough in-play damage to keep pitchers from pitching him without fear, because a 40.1% chase rate suggests he isn't drawing them into the zone with patience, and if hitters' counts don't improve, the contact advantage gets neutralized. Either a useful bench piece who earns his at-bats with the bat-to-ball, or a fringe regular whose ceiling is exactly what the projection already shows.

reports.name: Alex Bregman
reports.published_report:
The contact metrics are fine. The power is not.

Bregman's plate discipline is genuinely elite, a 21.8% chase rate and 16.4% whiff rate that rank in the 92nd and 87th percentiles respectively, but a 4.3% barrel rate and 88.2 mph average exit velocity tell you the bat isn't generating damage at a rate that matches the approach. ValuCast has him at 18 home runs across 709 plate appearances, which is a second-division offensive profile for a corner infielder, salvaged mainly by his 10.9% walk rate and 91st-percentile defense at third. If the contact quality doesn't recover, the discipline becomes a way to survive rather than a way to produce.

reports.name: Brock Wilken
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument, and it's not enough. Wilken is drawing 69 walks in 395 AAA plate appearances, an 18% clip that translates to roughly 13.5% at the MLB level, well above league average, but the contact is so bad that none of it converts: his .177 average at AAA sits in the 5th percentile among his peers, and a .228 BABIP suggests the ball isn't even finding holes when it does get put in play. The translated ISO of .144 lands right at league average, so there's no thump to bail out the batting average, and 114 strikeouts in that same sample make the hit tool look structural rather than streaky. If the contact ever firms up, there's a real on-base profile underneath this; if it doesn't, the walks buy him a bench role at best, and he's drifting down ValuCast's rankings for good reason.

Troy is hitting .307/.397/.449 through 205 plate appearances at AAA, which reads well until you translate it: the MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .132, against a translated average of .150, and the strikeout rate actually ticks up once the level discount applies. He walks enough, 26 in 205 plate appearances, that the on-base skills are genuine, but the power isn't there to force a team's hand. Now he's on the 10-day IL with a sprained right AC joint, which puts even the modest development window on hold. If the BABIP normalizes and the power doesn't grow, what's left is a fringe-regular profile built on contact rates that AAA won't necessarily export.

reports.name: Robert Arias
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.

reports.name: Garret Forrester
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it almost doesn't belong here. Thirty-two walks in 147 plate appearances across AAA & AA translates to a 13.2% MLB-equivalent walk rate, while the average big-league hitter sits at 8.5%, and his minor-league peer percentile is 99th. The power reads more modestly once you run it through the translation, a .169 ISO equivalent, but 7 home runs and a .255 ISO across AAA & AA on a .248 BABIP suggests the raw thump isn't borrowed from luck. The whole thing hinges on the strikeout rate holding, because at catcher, a 22% MLB-equivalent K rate is manageable if the plate discipline travels, and everything here collapses to org depth if the walks regress without the batting average filling in. Either a patient, borderline-playable big-league backstop or a waiver-wire name the moment the zone judgment slips.

If the command ever rounds into shape, there's a depth arm here; if it doesn't, the strikeouts just make the walks more expensive.

reports.name: Leonel Sequera
reports.published_report: The sample covers 79.7 IP in High-A, so confidence is low. Nothing in the profile gives him a dependable way through a lineup yet. Neither misses nor strikes separate in the strikeout-to-walk result. A rotation role is not supported by the current line; the floor is organizational depth or a low-leverage bullpen assignment.
